title: Osian's Pocket Watch Panic
markdown:
The Whispering Willow Inn sat in a valley where mist liked to settle like a grey cat that had found a lap. Osian Buttercup, a rabbit who loved everything just so and had a voice that could hush a market, straightened a perfectly white apron and scanned the dining room. Spotless. He had practised his greeting twenty times. The Inspector’s visit would be perfect, or it would not be an Osian visit at all.

Edie the weasel zipped past with a duster, quick as a blink. “Almost time. The carriage is just over the hill.”

“Being on time matters as much as a risen loaf,” Osian said. His ears stood at attention. Appearance was a kind of bread: if it fell, everything tasted of worry.

Inspector Sterling entered, a badger with quiet eyes and a talent for noticing the thing you had hoped was furniture. Osian offered a respectful nod that contained a small extra portion of dread, and began the tour.

“The dining room,” he said. “Forks and knives like a constellation. Tablecloths ironed until they nearly sing.” Sterling’s paw drifted near a salt shaker. Osian held his breath. The shaker survived. A small win, filed under miracles.

They moved through halls that smelled of lavender and beeswax. Osian opened a guest room where the bed looked like a well-behaved cloud. “Comfort, simply put. Tea brewed just so. Biscuits from our bakery — Great-Aunt Mildred’s recipe. She believed a good biscuit could mend most small problems.” Sterling considered the tin, then the tea set. Osian’s thoughts queued: too many biscuits? Not enough? Mildred had never been inspected by a badger.

Sterling nodded and gave nothing away. He ran a paw over a table, then looked down at the neat gardens. Osian’s heart kept its own hurried time. He always saved the pantry for last. It was his pride, his geometry of jam.

“And now,” he said, important again, “the heart of the Whispering Willow.”

Jars labelled in fancy writing lined the shelves. Flour and sugar stood in obedient piles. A tiny smudge of flour by the door caught his eye; Edie could see to that later. He reached into his waistcoat for his grandfather’s pocket watch, a habit at the end of any performance. His paw found lining. Nothing else.

A shiver went through his whiskers. The careful calm split. “The watch.” His voice, usually news from a far kingdom, wobbled like a wireless with a loose wire.

Edie’s nose twitched. “Oh, Osian.”

His eyes raked jars and sacks. “It was right here.” Dried herbs, usually a comfort, felt heavy. He pictured a headline no inn needed: Rabbit Baker Misplaces Time.

“It can’t have vanished.” Edie, caught in the weather of him, scrambled behind a potato sack and emerged powdered. She checked under apple crates; bruised apples made a break for freedom. Pip the mouse, ordinarily employed against pests, searched the tiles. Beatrice the badger, night manager and professional calm, peered behind a pickle barrel with an expression that suggested the barrel had disappointed her. The inn’s usual quiet became a mutter of urgent help.

Sterling stood still and watched the fuss. Osian’s professional mask slipped at one corner. Baking bread, which ought to have smelled like welcome, now smelled like irony.

Osian stopped searching. He looked at the Inspector. The broadcast voice had gone; what remained was a rabbit in a pantry. “It seems my pocket watch is gone. A lapse. I am sorry.”

The silence that followed had more body than any announcement he had ever made.

Sterling’s voice was soft as snow and twice as accurate. “Osian. When you thought I had arrived early, weren’t you winding it by the front door? You looked rather pleased with the ticking.”

Osian froze. He had been winding it. He had paced by the oak door, enjoying the little clicks, so eager for the inspection that the watch had gone back into the waistcoat without applying for a memory. In the panic, the obvious had taken the afternoon off. The watch, still ticking, was tucked in the inside lining, a cool circle of brass doing its job in the dark.

A sheepish grin reached his ears. He drew out the familiar metal. Oil and old brass rose from it like a small, private kitchen.

“Well,” Osian said, and the voice came back warmer, mocking itself just enough. “Our emergency appears to have been in the lining.” He held up the chain so it caught the pantry light. “The Whispering Willow remains standing. The apples, I regret, are less composed.”

Sterling smiled, a real one, and picked up a fallen apple. “A perfectly good apple.” He accepted a fresh biscuit when Osian offered it. Mildred, had she been present, would have called that a successful inspection and a wasted panic, which was nearly the same thing.

Edie brushed flour from her fur. Pip returned to professional pest thoughts. Beatrice closed the pickle barrel as if it had seen enough theatre. The watch ticked against Osian’s ribs, where it had been all along, and the mist outside settled again, a grey cat that had never left the lap.
characters: Osian Buttercup (a practical rabbit baker), Edie (a weasel friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
